parts.label: Understand
parts.title: Match the grader to the claim
parts.body:
Use a deterministic check when a result can be mechanically verified: valid schema, correct account ID, a forbidden tool call, or a known calculation. A rubric is needed when several responses can be acceptable and quality depends on factual support, completeness, or useful reasoning. Domain experts should set the rubric and review consequential cases. A model grader can make large-scale review affordable, but it must be compared with trusted human judgments before it influences a release gate.

A single score hides distinct risks. An answer may be well written and unsupported; another may be correct but omit an essential exception. Keep separate error categories and severity. For a source-grounded answer, ask whether each material claim is supported by the cited source, whether the source is current and accessible to the user, and whether the answer says when evidence is insufficient. Counting citations alone measures formatting.

Write the rubric with concrete score anchors and counterexamples. Allow partial credit where the task permits it, but identify failures that always block. Show graders the task context and authorised source without leaking an answer that merely invites surface matching.

example.title: Two different graders
example.body: A parser checks that every invoice output has an amount and currency in the required schema. An expert rubric checks whether a dispute letter accurately describes the contract and offers an appropriate next step. A parseable letter can still misstate the contract.

exercise.title: Build a grading plan
exercise.body: Choose three claims for an assistant: one mechanical, one factual, and one subjective. Assign a grader, expected evidence, failure severity, and an escalation path for ambiguous cases. Give one counterexample for each claim.

parts.label: Practice
parts.title: Calibrate a model judge against experts
parts.body:
Create a small, varied calibration set with clear successes, clear failures, and disputed cases. Ask two qualified people to score independently on a documented rubric, then discuss disagreements. Only after the human standard is clear should a model grader score the same cases. Compare its decisions with the adjudicated labels by category and severity. An overall agreement number can conceal a dangerous pattern, such as passing polished but unsupported answers.

For example, use a 0 to 2 factual-support rubric: 2 means every material claim is supported by the authorised source; 1 means a correct core answer has a minor unsupported detail or omission; 0 means a material claim contradicts or lacks the source. Define how missing sources and contradictory sources are treated. Report confusion cases, not only average score.

Revise the rubric or grader prompt when disagreement reveals ambiguity, then retest on fresh cases. Do not repeatedly tune on the same set and call the resulting agreement independent validation. Keep expert review on severe or uncertain cases and sample routine decisions as the system changes.

example.title: A thirty-case calibration
example.body: Two HR experts independently grade 30 answers and disagree on four. They consult the approved policy and adjudicate 20 as supported and 10 as materially unsupported. The model judge passes 18 of the 20 supported cases and wrongly fails two; it fails seven of the ten unsupported cases and wrongly passes three. Two of those three false passes invent eligibility exceptions, so the judge cannot control release even though it agrees on 25/30. The team clarifies the rubric, keeps human review, and tests the revised judge on a fresh, independently labelled set. These counts are illustrative; a small clean retest would still need production sampling.

exercise.title: Calibrate thirty answers
exercise.body: Write a 0 to 2 rubric for factual support and select 30 varied answers. Describe two independent expert passes, disagreement resolution, model-judge comparison, and the severe false-pass pattern that would bar the model judge from controlling release.

parts.label: Operate
parts.title: Read metrics without losing the failures
parts.body:
Pass rates need counts, denominators, and a case mix. A model that passes 90 of 100 cases may have failed every case in a ten-item high-risk category. Show performance by category and severity, plus uncertainty for small samples. Pairwise comparison can help choose between two acceptable drafts, but it does not replace a hard safety constraint. A statistically impressive average improvement may have little business value if it occurs only on easy cases.

When graders disagree, review the underlying cases before adjusting a threshold. Distinguish bad output from ambiguous expected behaviour, incorrect source material, and a flawed grader. Track both false passes and false failures in a small confusion matrix against adjudicated human labels. False passes are especially consequential when the grade controls a release or unattended action. Recalculate after changes and retain prior results so a new rubric does not appear to improve the model retroactively. OpenAI's evaluation guidance discusses model judges and grader design; the organisation must set its own severity-based acceptance rule.

For executive reporting, give a short table of task success, severe failures, human correction rate, grader disagreement, and cost or latency. Include a few representative error cases with the decision they imply. The point is to decide what to fix or exclude.

example.title: The average that concealed a block
example.body: A test shows 90% overall success, but all ten restricted-account cases fail. The release memo separates the categories, blocks account access, and funds the control fix. The total score does not justify that capability.

exercise.title: Audit an attractive score
exercise.body: Invent a 100-case result with a 90% overall pass rate and one unacceptable failure concentration. Show the counts by task category, what uncertainty remains, and the release decision. State what additional cases you would collect.

parts.label: Apply
parts.title: Commission a grading system you can audit
parts.body:
A CAIO does not need to write every grader. The CAIO needs to know what it can and cannot establish. Require a specification for each release-critical measure: task definition, input and source, grader type, rubric or exact assertion, sample selection, human calibration, uncertainty, owner, and change control. Keep the raw cases and decisions available for review under appropriate privacy protections.

Before trusting automation, commission a blind audit of model-grader false passes on high-impact cases. If experts disagree substantially, clarify policy and expected outcomes first. If the grader is unreliable on a severe slice, route that slice to humans or hold the capability. Recalibrate when task mix, model, or policy changes. A model judge that was adequate for tone may be unsuitable for privacy or financial correctness.

Use a decision rule that connects errors to scope. A release can proceed for well-tested routine drafting while contract interpretation remains review-only. Document who can override the grade, what evidence is needed, and how overrides are examined for patterns.

example.title: A split release
example.body: Automated format checks pass, and a calibrated judge performs adequately on routine summaries. Experts find false passes on contract exceptions. The team launches draft summaries with staff approval while withholding unattended contract advice.

exercise.title: Write a grader acceptance sheet
exercise.body: For one release-critical rubric, state acceptable human agreement, false-pass review, calibration set, retest frequency, override owner, and the condition that sends cases back to expert review. Use organisation-specific thresholds and justify them.
